input:
It is important to note that the staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 17%, a figure that has been carefully considered in light of the project's overall requirements. While a lower alternative has been suggested to the steering group, it is felt that this would not adequately support the successful delivery of the project, particularly during its crucial early stages. The initial phase of the project is characterised by a range of supervision-intensive activities, including setting out, expediting, and the establishment of the first work fronts, all of which require appropriate staffing levels from the very outset in order to ensure that momentum is maintained.

Furthermore, adopting a lower ramp would not actually reduce the underlying cost; rather, it would simply defer recruitment into the construction period itself, where the same positions would need to be filled under significantly greater time pressure. This could potentially lead to compromises in candidate quality, thereby undermining the project's long-term prospects. By contrast, holding the ramp at 17% provides a more robust and sustainable basis for delivery, and the figure can subsequently be re-tested at FID once the awarded programme is available. The detailed build-up is provided in the project's cost table, and stakeholders are encouraged to refer to it for further information regarding the full establishment profile and associated recruitment assumptions going forward
target:
The staffing ramp for the upgrade project is set at 17%, and the lower figure proposed to the steering group is not accepted. The defence of the higher figure rests on the order in which the work arrives. The first activities on the upgrade project are the supervision-heavy ones: setting out, expediting and the opening work fronts each need their full staffing from the start, and a ramp set lower staffs those activities in proportion to a build-up they do not follow. The shortfall appears at the front of the programme, where float is smallest.

A lower ramp does not remove the cost of the posts. It moves recruitment into the construction period, where the same posts are filled later, under time pressure, and against the same start dates. The steering group is therefore asked to hold 17% and to re-test the figure at FID, when the awarded programme replaces the estimate programme as the basis for the profile. The post-by-post build-up stands in the project's cost table and is not repeated here. The steering group is asked to settle the profile alone, and to settle it while the lead times on the scarcer grades still allow the ramp to be met as drawn, rather than recovered after the event with the early activities under way
